Those lead to different infrastructure: step-indexed traces and replay buffers versus a dense reward scorer. Without isolating the mechanism, teams will copy the surface recipe (GRPO plus turns) without the component that actually matters.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Do rubric-based judges remain discriminative as the policy improves and learns to satisfy the rubric surface rather than the underlying task?
deep_dives.why: The claim that rubric judging reduces reward hacking is measured on an untrained or lightly trained policy. If human agreement decays under iterated pressure, then rubric quality is not a one-time artifact but a continuously maintained, adversarially contested component, and any training pipeline built on rubric rewards needs a rubric-refresh loop with its own cadence and cost.

deep_dives.why: The entire value proposition of an AI scientist rests on this transfer. If replication performance is orthogonal to discovery, then replication benchmarks are a proxy metric that can be maximized indefinitely without producing scientific output — a measurement trap for anyone funding or building on the replication task space.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Defines open-endedness as a system's ability to continually generate artifacts that are both novel and learnable to an observer.
deep_dives.why: The definition is testable in principle but brittle in practice: any measurable novelty score becomes an objective once a policy trains against it. Resolving how to specify the observer and rotate or hold it out determines whether open-endedness can be an evaluation axis at all, or whether it must remain descriptive.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Edward Hughes
  • Channel: Machine Learning Street Talk
  • Main topic: Training AI agents to replicate scientific research and achieve open-endedness
  • Purpose: To explain the technical and philosophical foundations of training AI scientist systems for open-ended scientific discovery and paper replication. Edward Hughes, co-founder and chief scientist at Inherent, discusses the transition from individual AI intelligence to collective intelligence and the design of AI scientist systems. He covers the Faraday paper on training AI scientists to replicate machine learning and AI-for-science research papers using coding agents, GRPO, and automated rubric-based judges. The conversation explores open-endedness, the limits of optimization, evolutionary algorithms, and the importance of open-ended task spaces and evaluation in building autonomous scientific discovery agents.

Topic Map

From Individual Intelligence to Collective Intelligence

  • Explanation: The shift from single-agent capability to collective intelligence across multiple interacting agents and humans.
  • Key claims:
    • The next era is collective intelligence rather than individual intelligence.
    • AI by itself is meaningless without interaction with the wider ecosystem and scientific progress.
  • Examples:
    • Move 37 in Go was innovative without being creative in the true sense.
  • Terminology:
    • collective intelligence
    • recursive self-improvement
    • phase transition
  • Why it matters: Defines the paradigm shift required for autonomous AI systems to drive scientific progress.

Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research (The Faraday Paper)

  • Explanation: Introducing Faraday, a 27B parameter AI scientist agent that leverages coding agents as tools to replicate machine learning and AI-for-science papers.
  • Key claims:
    • Faraday outperforms frontier models like Claude and Codex on paper replication tasks.
    • Prompt optimization using automated judging loops improves agent performance on long-horizon tasks.
  • Examples:
    • Replicating 300 AI and ML papers published between 1990 and 2026.
  • Terminology:
    • Faraday
    • GRPO
    • per-task rubric generator
    • rubric-based judge
    • Replica task space
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that open-weight models with proper scaffolding can perform rigorous scientific replication.

Open-Endedness and the Limits of Optimization

  • Explanation: Exploring the relationship between open-endedness, optimization, constraints, and why greatness cannot be planned.
  • Key claims:
    • Optimization is the wrong tool for creativity because it relies on known objectives.
    • Open-endedness requires moving from solving known problems to discovering new problems and questions.
    • Constraints act as a form of abstract knowledge that enables creative discovery.
  • Examples:
    • AlphaGo optimized within a fixed rule set, whereas open-ended systems discover new domains.
  • Terminology:
    • open-endedness
    • optimization
    • constraints
    • acceptation
    • observer-dependent novelty
  • Why it matters: Provides a theoretical foundation for building systems capable of superhuman open-ended innovation.

Organizational Design and Harness Engineering

  • Explanation: Drawing analogies between human organizational evolution, harness engineering, and AI agent architectures.
  • Key claims:
    • Harness engineering is crucial for guiding AI agents, but too much hardcoding limits generalization.
    • Recursive self-improvement should happen at the company level through interacting human-AI teams.
  • Examples:
    • Comparing the industrial revolution and electric dynamos to modern AI agent engineering.
  • Terminology:
    • harness engineering
    • Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM)
    • turn-level credit assignment
    • per-task rubric
  • Why it matters: Bridges machine learning agent design with organizational economics and evolutionary biology.

Key Points

Faraday Agent Architecture

  • Explanation: Faraday uses a Qwen 3.6-27B base model combined with Codex as a tool, optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rubric-based judging.
  • Evidence: Performance evaluation charts on ML and AI-for-science held-out tasks.
  • Practical implication: Enables open-weight models to compete with or beat proprietary frontier models on complex scientific tasks.

The Role of Rubrics in Evaluation

  • Explanation: Instead of relying on single binary rewards or simple test cases, Faraday uses per-task rubric generators and LLM judges to assess visual fidelity, claim reproduction, implementation fidelity, experimental depth, and scientific integrity.
  • Evidence: Figure 3 showing higher human agreement and lower noise with rubric-based judging.
  • Practical implication: Reduces reward hacking and provides robust multi-dimensional evaluation for non-verifiable agent tasks.

Turn-Level Credit Assignment

  • Explanation: Assigning reward credit at the individual turn level rather than just the final rollout prevents credit assignment collapse in long-horizon RL tasks.
  • Evidence: Ablation plots showing stability improvements when turn-level credit assignment is used.
  • Practical implication: Stabilizes training for multi-turn coding and scientific experimentation agents.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Faraday Replication Pipeline

  • How it works: Generates replication tasks from published papers, executes them using a coding agent in a container, and evaluates outputs using rubric-based judges.
  • Components:
    • Replica task space
    • Faraday policy with Codex tool
    • Per-task rubric generator
    • Rubric-based judge
    • GRPO optimizer
  • When to use: When training AI agents to execute complex, multi-step scientific paper replication tasks.

Open-Endedness Definition

  • How it works: Defines open-endedness as a system's ability to continually generate artifacts that are both novel and learnable to an observer.
  • Components:
    • System producing artifacts
    • Observer evaluating novelty
    • Observer evaluating learnability
  • When to use: When assessing whether an AI system is capable of unbounded cumulative discovery.

Examples & Case Studies

Faraday was evaluated on 68 held-out AI-for-science tasks against frontier models like Claude, Codex, and Qwen.

  • Illustrates: The effectiveness of training open-weight models with targeted tool use and rubric-based reinforcement learning.
  • Lesson: Specialized agent scaffolding and careful reward design can allow smaller open models to outperform larger closed models.

Dmitry Bahdanau added an attention mechanism to a machine translation model initially just as a heuristic component.

  • Illustrates: How foundational discoveries often start as seemingly minor architectural modifications that later become universal.
  • Lesson: True innovation often comes from breaking existing constraints in unexpected ways.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Rubric-based judges significantly reduce noise and hacking compared to binary verification.
    • Turn-level credit assignment is essential for stabilizing RL training on multi-turn coding agents.
    • Open-weight models like Qwen-27B can achieve top-tier scientific performance with proper harness engineering.
  • Strategic:
    • Open-endedness and discovery are more fundamental to AGI than static optimization against fixed benchmarks.
    • Collective intelligence and human-AI collaboration will dominate individual agent capabilities.
    • Scaling task diversity is more important than scaling model size alone for scientific discovery agents.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we avoid good-hacking when scaling evaluation rubrics for autonomous discovery?
    • What is the equivalent of OKRs for recursive self-improving AI agent organizations?
    • How can open-ended agent systems autonomously discover valid scientific domains without human curation?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Faraday outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out paper replication tasks. (empirical)
  • GRPO stabilizes reinforcement learning by computing group-relative advantages without a separate value network. (technical)

Notable Quotes

"How do we start to build AI scientist systems that go beyond simply answering questions that we pose and start to ask the kinds of questions that lead to open-ended creative discovery?" (at 0:00) "The replicability of papers is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, ensuring the reliability of existing results and providing a base for further experiments." (at 0:30) "That kind of open-ended invention is the mechanism by which human individuals and society at large accumulates new knowledge and technology." (at 151:50)

Compressed Summary

  • Faraday trains a 27B model to replicate scientific papers using coding agents and GRPO.
  • Per-task rubric generators and LLM judges replace brittle binary verification.
  • Turn-level credit assignment prevents RL collapse on long-horizon tasks.
  • Open-endedness requires systems to generate artifacts that are both novel and learnable to an observer.
  • Keywords: ai-scientist, replication, open-endedness, reinforcement-learning, rubrics
  • Core insight: Building an AI scientist requires moving beyond static optimization to open-ended task generation, rubric-based evaluation, and multi-turn credit assignment.

  - Prompt optimization using automated judging loops improves agent performance on long-horizon tasks.
- **Examples**:
  - Replicating 300 AI and ML papers published between 1990 and 2026.
- **Terminology**:
  - Faraday
  - GRPO
  - per-task rubric generator
  - rubric-based judge
  - Replica task space
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that open-weight models with proper scaffolding can perform rigorous scientific replication.
### Open-Endedness and the Limits of Optimization
- **Explanation**: Exploring the relationship between open-endedness, optimization, constraints, and why greatness cannot be planned.
- **Key claims**:
  - Optimization is the wrong tool for creativity because it relies on known objectives.
  - Open-endedness requires moving from solving known problems to discovering new problems and questions.
  - Constraints act as a form of abstract knowledge that enables creative discovery.
- **Examples**:
  - AlphaGo optimized within a fixed rule set, whereas open-ended systems discover new domains.
- **Terminology**:
  - open-endedness
  - optimization
  - constraints
  - acceptation
  - observer-dependent novelty
- **Why it matters**: Provides a theoretical foundation for building systems capable of superhuman open-ended innovation.
### Organizational Design and Harness Engineering
- **Explanation**: Drawing analogies between human organizational evolution, harness engineering, and AI agent architectures.
- **Key claims**:
  - Harness engineering is crucial for guiding AI agents, but too much hardcoding limits generalization.
  - Recursive self-improvement should happen at the company level through interacting human-AI teams.
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing the industrial revolution and electric dynamos to modern AI agent engineering.
- **Terminology**:
  - harness engineering
  - Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM)
  - turn-level credit assignment
  - per-task rubric
- **Why it matters**: Bridges machine learning agent design with organizational economics and evolutionary biology.
## Key Points
### Faraday Agent Architecture
- **Explanation**: Faraday uses a Qwen 3.6-27B base model combined with Codex as a tool, optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rubric-based judging.
- **Evidence**: Performance evaluation charts on ML and AI-for-science held-out tasks.
- **Practical implication**: Enables open-weight models to compete with or beat proprietary frontier models on complex scientific tasks.
### The Role of Rubrics in Evaluation
- **Explanation**: Instead of relying on single binary rewards or simple test cases, Faraday uses per-task rubric generators and LLM judges to assess visual fidelity, claim reproduction, implementation fidelity, experimental depth, and scientific integrity.
- **Evidence**: Figure 3 showing higher human agreement and lower noise with rubric-based judging.
- **Practical implication**: Reduces reward hacking and provides robust multi-dimensional evaluation for non-verifiable agent tasks.
### Turn-Level Credit Assignment
- **Explanation**: Assigning reward credit at the individual turn level rather than just the final rollout prevents credit assignment collapse in long-horizon RL tasks.
- **Evidence**: Ablation plots showing stability improvements when turn-level credit assignment is used.
- **Practical implication**: Stabilizes training for multi-turn coding and scientific experimentation agents.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Faraday Replication Pipeline
- **How it works**: Generates replication tasks from published papers, executes them using a coding agent in a container, and evaluates outputs using rubric-based judges.
- **Components**:
  - Replica task space
  - Faraday policy with Codex tool
  - Per-task rubric generator
  - Rubric-based judge
  - GRPO optimizer
- **When to use**: When training AI agents to execute complex, multi-step scientific paper replication tasks.
### Open-Endedness Definition
- **How it works**: Defines open-endedness as a system's ability to continually generate artifacts that are both novel and learnable to an observer.
- **Components**:
  - System producing artifacts
  - Observer evaluating novelty
  - Observer evaluating learnability
- **When to use**: When assessing whether an AI system is capable of unbounded cumulative discovery.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Faraday was evaluated on 68 held-out AI-for-science tasks against frontier models like Claude, Codex, and Qwen.
- **Illustrates**: The effectiveness of training open-weight models with targeted tool use and rubric-based reinforcement learning.
- **Lesson**: Specialized agent scaffolding and careful reward design can allow smaller open models to outperform larger closed models.
### Dmitry Bahdanau added an attention mechanism to a machine translation model initially just as a heuristic component.
- **Illustrates**: How foundational discoveries often start as seemingly minor architectural modifications that later become universal.
- **Lesson**: True innovation often comes from breaking existing constraints in unexpected ways.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Rubric-based judges significantly reduce noise and hacking compared to binary verification.
  - Turn-level credit assignment is essential for stabilizing RL training on multi-turn coding agents.
  - Open-weight models like Qwen-27B can achieve top-tier scientific performance with proper harness engineering.
- **Strategic**:
  - Open-endedness and discovery are more fundamental to AGI than static optimization against fixed benchmarks.
  - Collective intelligence and human-AI collaboration will dominate individual agent capabilities.
  - Scaling task diversity is more important than scaling model size alone for scientific discovery agents.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we avoid good-hacking when scaling evaluation rubrics for autonomous discovery?
  - What is the equivalent of OKRs for recursive self-improving AI agent organizations?
  - How can open-ended agent systems autonomously discover valid scientific domains without human curation?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Faraday outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out paper replication tasks. (empirical)
- GRPO stabilizes reinforcement learning by computing group-relative advantages without a separate value network. (technical)
## Notable Quotes
> "How do we start to build AI scientist systems that go beyond simply answering questions that we pose and start to ask the kinds of questions that lead to open-ended creative discovery?" (at 0:00)
> "The replicability of papers is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, ensuring the reliability of existing results and providing a base for further experiments." (at 0:30)
> "That kind of open-ended invention is the mechanism by which human individuals and society at large accumulates new knowledge and technology." (at 151:50)
## Compressed Summary
- Faraday trains a 27B model to replicate scientific papers using coding agents and GRPO.
- Per-task rubric generators and LLM judges replace brittle binary verification.
- Turn-level credit assignment prevents RL collapse on long-horizon tasks.
- Open-endedness requires systems to generate artifacts that are both novel and learnable to an observer.

- **Core insight**: Building an AI scientist requires moving beyond static optimization to open-ended task generation, rubric-based evaluation, and multi-turn credit assignment.
